::: {.lesson-section #what-is-an-accelerometer}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 1.1</p>
<h2>What Is an Accelerometer?</h2>

An accelerometer is a sensor that records acceleration over time, commonly along three axes. In human movement research, the device does not directly "know" whether a person is exercising, sitting, or asleep. Researchers combine the recorded signal with a documented processing method, a wear location, and a study protocol to derive interpretable outcomes.

The raw signal is commonly stored in gravitational units (*g*) or metres per second squared (*m/s²*). Later in the pipeline, it can be summarized as **ENMO** (*Euclidean Norm Minus One*): calculate the Euclidean norm of the three axes, subtract 1 *g*, and commonly truncate negative values to zero. Intensity summaries such as **MVPA** are not direct sensor readings; they are derived after applying thresholds or algorithms to processed data.

<strong>Technical clarification:</strong> The video's spoken explanation simplifies ENMO. ENMO is the Euclidean norm of the three acceleration axes minus 1 <em>g</em>; negative values are commonly truncated to zero. It is not calculated by subtracting 1 <em>g</em> independently from each axis or from an unspecified “signal.”

::: {.lesson-section #what-can-accelerometers-measure}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 1.2</p>
<h2>What Can Accelerometers Measure?</h2>

Accelerometer recordings can support estimates of several dimensions of movement behavior. The exact outcome depends on the device, placement, algorithm, calibration, and processing choices. Common outcomes include physical-activity volume and intensity, sedentary time, body posture, activity type, and sleep-wake timing.

<div class="video-summary">
<p class="video-summary__label">Quick summary <span>Brief review</span></p>
<p>Accelerometer data can support estimates of activity volume and intensity, sedentary time, posture, activity type, and sleep–wake timing. Every estimate depends on the device, placement, algorithm, calibration, and processing choices, so the method must be reported with the outcome.</p>
</div>
<!-- transcript:lesson-1-2-what-can-accelerometers-measure -->
<details class="video-transcript" data-video="lesson-1-2-what-can-accelerometers-measure">
<summary>Read the full video transcript <span>Timestamped · English</span></summary>
<p class="video-transcript__tools"><a href="captions/lesson-1-2-what-can-accelerometers-measure.vtt" download>Download English captions (.vtt)</a></p>
<div class="video-transcript__body">
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:00</span> In the last lesson, we saw that an accelerometer records just one thing. Acceleration over time. It doesn&#x27;t know whether you&#x27;re walking, sitting, or asleep. So here&#x27;s the natural question. If all it stores is a raw signal, what can we actually measure from it? The answer is</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:16</span> quite a lot, as long as we&#x27;re honest about how we got there. Think of the raw signal as a single source. Depending on how we process it and where the device was worn, that one source can support estimates in five broad domains. Physical</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:32</span> activity: how much you move. Sedentary behavior: estimates of waking time spent in low-energy sitting, reclining, or lying. Sleep–wake behavior: estimates of when sleep and wake occur and how they are patterned. Body posture: whether you&#x27;re sitting, standing, or lying. And activity</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:49</span> type: what movement you&#x27;re doing. Keep one word in mind for all five: estimate. Every outcome depends on the device, the placement, the algorithm, the calibration, and the processing. Change any of those and the number changes. Total movement can be summarized using measures</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:06</span> such as mean acceleration, estimated energy expenditure in kilocalories, MET-based intensity or volume measures, or step counts. Processed data may also be classified into low movement or inactive, light, moderate, and vigorous categories. Do not automatically interpret</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:23</span> all low movement time as sedentary behavior. The flip side of activity is what happens when movement is very low. An intensity-based method can estimate low movement or inactive time and interruptions in that pattern. To estimate sitting time, sitting breaks, and</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:39</span> sedentary bouts more specifically, we need posture-sensitive processing and an appropriate placement, often the thigh and sometimes the trunk. A wrist monitor may detect low wrist movement, but it cannot by itself prove that a person is sitting. A thigh-worn monitor,</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:55</span> combined with a validated algorithm, can more directly classify sitting, standing, and lying. Placement and algorithm determine what we can trust. Because many people now wear monitors around the clock, algorithms can estimate sleep-wake timing and duration. Depending</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:11</span> on the algorithm and whether a sleep diary or sleep opportunity window is available, they may also estimate sleep onset and offset, midpoint, latency, efficiency, and movement-based fragmentation. These are algorithm-derived estimates of sleep-wake behavior, not a clinical</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:26</span> diagnosis, and they do not replace polysomnography when a clinical sleep evaluation is required. Some workflows go further and try to label the type of movement, walking, running, cycling, stair-stepping. This is harder and much more algorithm-specific than simple volume or intensity,</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:45</span> and it&#x27;s worth being clear about the limits. An accelerometer measures motion, not meaning. It doesn&#x27;t know why you moved, it can&#x27;t weigh the load you carried, and depending on the device and placement, it may miss activities like cycling or swimming. Treat every output</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:59</span> as an estimate to be documented, not a fact the sensor simply read off. So five domains from one signal, physical activity, sedentary behavior, sleep–wake, body posture, and activity type. Each is an estimate shaped by placement, algorithm, and</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">03:17</span> processing.</p>
</div>
</details>


::: {.table-scroll}
| Domain | Examples of potential outcomes | Interpretation note |
|---|---|---|
| Physical activity | Movement volume, energy expenditure, steps, light activity, MVPA, vigorous activity | Estimates are method-dependent; report the processing approach and thresholds. |
| Sedentary behavior | Sedentary time, breaks, and accumulated sedentary bouts | Posture-sensitive estimates require an appropriate placement and algorithm. |
| Sleep-wake behavior | Sleep duration, onset, offset, midpoint, latency, efficiency, fragmentation | These are algorithm-derived estimates, not a clinical diagnosis. |
| Body posture | Sitting, standing, lying | Usually depends on placement such as thigh or trunk sensors. |
| Activity type | Walking, running, cycling, stair-stepping | Activity-type classification is more algorithm-specific than volume and intensity summaries. |
:::

::: {.lesson-section #placement-and-protocol}
<p class="section-kicker">Lesson 1.3</p>
<h2>Placement and Protocol Decisions</h2>

Before a monitor is initialized, the study team must choose the device model, wear location, start and stop dates, instructions for participants, and criteria for evaluating whether a recording is usable. These decisions affect participant burden and the outcomes that can be validly interpreted.

Different monitor placements are useful for different questions. A thigh-worn monitor may support posture classification, while wrist placement often improves comfort and continuous wear. The best placement follows the research question and protocol rather than a universal rule.

<div class="video-summary">
<p class="video-summary__label">Quick summary <span>Brief review</span></p>
<p>Wear location and protocol determine what movement is captured, which algorithms are appropriate, and how likely participants are to comply. Select wrist, hip, thigh, trunk, ankle, or low-back placement according to the research question, then document attachment, timing, instructions, and usability criteria.</p>
</div>
<!-- transcript:module1-placement-correct-wear -->
<details class="video-transcript" data-video="module1-placement-correct-wear">
<summary>Read the full video transcript <span>Timestamped · English</span></summary>
<p class="video-transcript__tools"><a href="captions/module1-placement-correct-wear.vtt" download>Download English captions (.vtt)</a></p>
<div class="video-transcript__body">
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:00</span> In this module, you&#x27;ll see how accelerometers capture continuous movement signals and how those signals are processed into estimates of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep-wake patterns. The device doesn&#x27;t directly know what someone is doing. Data quality starts with the protocol and with wearing the device in the right position, with the right orientation, and a snug fit. An accelerometer records acceleration over time, often along three axes, creating a stream of raw signal rather than a ready-made behavior label.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:30</span> Researchers then combine that raw signal with processing decisions, wear location, and study protocol to turn recordings into usable data products. Those choices support estimates such as ENMO, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, sedentary time, posture, activity type, and sleep-wake timing. Depending on the study setup, accelerometers can support estimates of movement volume and intensity, sedentary behavior, and sleep-wake timing.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">00:57</span> Some placements and analytic approaches can also support estimates of posture and activity type. What you can estimate depends on the device, placement, algorithm, calibration, and processing choices used in the study. Placement matters because the same device captures different movement patterns at the wrist, hip, or waist, thigh, low back, chest, and ankle.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:18</span> Wrist placement is common for continuous wear, while hip and waist placement is often used for ambulatory activity patterns, and thigh placement can be especially useful for posture-sensitive outcomes. Low back, chest, and ankle placements can support more specific research questions, so the best location depends on what the study needs to estimate. No matter where the device is worn, the same three rules apply. Right position, right orientation, and snug fit.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">01:45</span> A recording can look technically successful and still be unusable. If the strap is loose, the device rotates, or it sits on the wrong body location. For wrist placement, wear the device on the non-dominant wrist. Position it correctly, keep the face oriented outward, and use a one-finger check to confirm a snug fit. A common mistake is a loose strap that slides or rotates around the wrist. That can change orientation and reduce confidence in the wear data.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:13</span> Correct it by tightening the strap so the device stays stable in place without pinching. For hip or waist placement, position the device at the side of the hip, aligned with the knee, and keep it flat against the body. The common mistake is drift toward the front or back, or a loose belt that lets the device move away from the correct side position.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:32</span> Correct it by aligning the device with the side of the hip bone, and tightening the belt for a snug fit. Also note that removing it for sleep or bathing may reduce wear time. For thigh placement, attach the device to the front mid-thigh, midway between the hip and knee, using a medical adhesive patch.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">02:50</span> A common mistake is peeling tape edges or a partial lift-off, which can let the device shift away from the intended position and angle. Correct it by pressing firmly and sealing all edges. This placement can be especially useful for posture-sensitive outcomes and activity classification. For low back placement, wear the device on a waist belt centered over the lower spine so it sits flat and stable.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">03:13</span> The common mistake is an off-center position or a loose belt that lets the device tilt and shift during movement. Correct it by re-centering the device on the spine, and tightening the belt enough to keep the unit flat against the body. For chest placement, position the device at the center of the chest over the sternum, using an elastic torso strap.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">03:35</span> A loose strap is the common mistake here because it allows tilt or rotation, so the device no longer stays flat and centered. Correct it by tightening the strap until the device is flat, stable, and centered. For ankle placement, fasten the device just above the ankle bone with a snug fit so it stays in a firm, stable position.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">03:54</span> The common mistake is a loose strap that rotates around the ankle and changes the intended position during walking or rest. Correct it by securing the strap just above the ankle bone. This placement can support locomotion studies and continuous wear, but in some young-child protocols, it may have limits for separating sedentary time and sleep.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">04:13</span> There&#x27;s no single best placement for every study. The right choice depends on the research question, protocol, and the outcomes your team needs to estimate. Before data collection, confirm the wear schedule, sampling frequency, valid-day criteria, non-wear algorithm, reporting units, and thresholds with the study lead.</p>
<p><span class="transcript-time">04:33</span> Then remember the core rule. Right position, right orientation, snug fit. Next you&#x27;ll cover programming and downloading.</p>
</div>
</details>


<h3>Quick Reference: Placement Planning</h3>

::: {.table-scroll}
| Placement | Good fit when the study needs... | Main planning risk |
|---|---|---|
| Wrist | High compliance, 24-hour wear, broad activity/sleep workflows | Intensity estimates and cut-points must match wrist placement. |
| Hip/waist | Ambulatory activity volume and historical comparability | Lower comfort and removal during sleep/bathing may reduce wear time. |
| Thigh | Posture-sensitive outcomes such as sitting/standing/lying | Attachment method and skin comfort must be planned carefully. |
| Chest/trunk | Trunk acceleration and some gait/posture applications | More obtrusive; not the default for many free-living studies. |
| Ankle | Locomotion in infants/toddlers or populations where hip/wrist are limited | Sleep vs sedentary separation may be difficult. |
| Low back | Balance and some whole-body movement applications | Adherence and belt attachment need protocol attention. |
:::

<details class="evidence-details">
<summary>Evidence details: placement strengths and limitations</summary>

::: {.table-scroll}
| Placement | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| Wrist ([Doherty et al., 2017](references.html#ref-doherty-2017)) | Large-scale wrist-worn protocols have been used successfully in population assessment. Participants may wear wrist-worn devices for longer periods than hip-worn devices ([Kerr et al., 2017](references.html#ref-kerr-2017)). | Sometimes less accurate than hip placement for selected physical-activity estimates ([Kerr et al., 2017](references.html#ref-kerr-2017)). |
| Chest ([Nazarahari & Rouhani, 2018](references.html#ref-nazarahari-2018)) | Chest-derived acceleration can reflect physical activity intensity and has been used to detect postures and walking modalities ([Mukaino et al., 2022](references.html#ref-mukaino-2022); [Nazarahari & Rouhani, 2018](references.html#ref-nazarahari-2018)). | Trunk movement measurement with a chest-mounted accelerometer may be less easy to implement than wrist-worn protocols ([Mukaino et al., 2022](references.html#ref-mukaino-2022)). |
| Low back ([Williamson et al., 2026](references.html#ref-williamson-2026)) | Commonly used for balance assessment and whole-body movement applications ([Ghislieri et al., 2019](references.html#ref-ghislieri-2019)). | Participant adherence can be challenging in skin-taped or body-worn protocols ([Schneller et al., 2017](references.html#ref-schneller-2017)). |
| Hip ([Migueles et al., 2017](references.html#ref-migueles-2017)) | Hip placement has strong historical use and can reflect energy expenditure well in laboratory and locomotive activities ([Hildebrand et al., 2014](references.html#ref-hildebrand-2014)). | Hip placement may be perceived as less comfortable and more socially obtrusive than wrist placement, lowering wear-time compliance in some groups ([Scott et al., 2017](references.html#ref-scott-2017)). |
| Thigh ([Kozey-Keadle et al., 2011](references.html#ref-kozey-keadle-2011)) | Thigh inclination can classify sitting more accurately than pelvis inclination, and thigh-based algorithms have been developed for activities such as stair walking and cycling ([Peterson et al., 2015](references.html#ref-peterson-2015); [Skotte et al., 2014](references.html#ref-skotte-2014)). | Attachment may require tape solutions that can loosen with activity, clothing changes, or participant discomfort ([Arvidsson et al., 2019](references.html#ref-arvidsson-2019)). |
| Ankle ([Dorris et al., 2025](references.html#ref-dorris-2025)) | Can support continuous 24-hour collection and may capture locomotion when hip or wrist placement is limited ([Campbell et al., 2021](references.html#ref-campbell-2021)). | May have difficulty differentiating sedentary time from sleep in young children ([Hager et al., 2016](references.html#ref-hager-2016)). |
:::

</details>

<h3>Device Selection Checklist</h3>

Device specifications vary by model, firmware, configuration, and date. Do not select or initialize a monitor from a brand-level comparison alone. Record the exact model and the current manufacturer source used for the decision.

::: {.table-scroll}
| Device family example | Common research role | Verify and record before use |
|---|---|---|
| ActiGraph | Raw acceleration and count-based research workflows | Exact model, dynamic range, sample rate, storage, battery, water protection, wear accessories, firmware, and ActiLife compatibility |
| Axivity | Configurable raw-acceleration research workflows | Exact model, recording configuration, storage, battery estimate, enclosure, wear method, firmware, and reader/software compatibility |
| GENEActiv | Wrist-worn raw-acceleration and 24-hour protocols | Exact model, sample rate, recording duration, water protection, firmware, wear instructions, and export format |
| activPAL | Thigh-worn posture and activity classification | Exact model, attachment method, recording configuration, battery/storage limits, water protection, and analysis software |
| Fibion | Body-worn activity and sedentary-behavior workflows | Exact model, placement, sample rate, recording duration, water protection, and compatible processing workflow |
:::

For the study record, save the source URL or manual title, model number, firmware/software version, and date verified. If a specification cannot be confirmed for the exact model, mark it unresolved rather than borrowing a value from another device.

::: {.decision-panel .slim}
<div>
<p class="section-kicker">Protocol review</p>
<h2>Confirm decisions before recording.</h2>
</div>
<p>Confirm the wear schedule, sampling frequency, valid-day criteria, non-wear algorithm, reporting units, and thresholds with the study's principal investigator or data lead. Prior cohort protocols are examples, not defaults for every study.</p>
:::

<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-mini-decision-draft-q1" value="d"> D. Adults will wear the verified exact-model monitor at the protocol-approved location for seven days to estimate the stated compatible outcome; the draft gives wear and removal times, attachment, water, charging or return, and problem-reporting instructions, records the model-source verification date, and assigns first quality review to the data manager.</label>

::: {.lesson-section #knowledge-check}
<p class="section-kicker">Wrap-up</p>
<h2>Knowledge Check</h2>

<form class="scored-quiz" data-quiz-id="module-1-knowledge-check" novalidate>
<fieldset data-answer="b" data-explanation="MVPA is an estimate derived from acceleration after applying a documented processing method and threshold; it is not directly sensed by the monitor.">
<legend><span>1</span> A report says, “The accelerometer measured 42 minutes of MVPA.” What important distinction is missing?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q1" value="a"> A. MVPA is the monitor's battery-life setting.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q1" value="b"> B. MVPA is estimated from acceleration with a documented method and threshold, not directly sensed by the monitor.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q1" value="c"> C. MVPA can be reported only when the device is thigh-worn.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q1" value="d"> D. The report should replace minutes with raw-axis units because MVPA and raw acceleration are identical.</label>
<p class="scored-quiz__feedback" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
</fieldset>

<fieldset data-answer="c" data-explanation="Stop and verify that the metric, threshold, and validation evidence match wrist placement and the study population. Do not transfer a hip threshold silently.">
<legend><span>2</span> A wrist-worn protocol uses a threshold developed for the hip. What should the analyst do before interpreting the result?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q2" value="a"> A. Use it unchanged because thresholds transfer across all body locations.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q2" value="b"> B. Double the threshold to compensate for wrist movement.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q2" value="c"> C. Stop and verify that the metric, threshold, and validation evidence match wrist placement and the study population.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q2" value="d"> D. Remove the wear-location information from the report.</label>
<p class="scored-quiz__feedback" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
</fieldset>

<fieldset data-answer="a" data-explanation="Placement and the posture-classification method are central. A thigh placement may be appropriate, but the choice must follow the protocol and validation evidence.">
<legend><span>3</span> A study wants to distinguish sitting from standing. Which planning decision deserves special attention?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q3" value="a"> A. Choose a placement and validated posture-classification method suited to that outcome, with thigh placement considered when supported.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q3" value="b"> B. Choose the brightest device display so participants can see it.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q3" value="c"> C. Use any wrist threshold because low wrist movement proves sitting.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q3" value="d"> D. Decide placement only after the data have been collected.</label>
<p class="scored-quiz__feedback" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
</fieldset>

<fieldset data-answer="d" data-explanation="Save the exact model and specification, the manufacturer source or manual, the firmware and software context, and the date verified so the decision remains traceable.">
<legend><span>4</span> What evidence should be saved when the team records a device specification?</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q4" value="a"> A. The device brand alone.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q4" value="b"> B. A colleague's memory of a similar model.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q4" value="c"> C. Only the value copied into the protocol, without its source or date.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="module-1-knowledge-check-q4" value="d"> D. The exact model and specification, manufacturer source or manual, firmware/software context, and verification date.</label>
<p class="scored-quiz__feedback" aria-live="polite" hidden></p>
</fieldset>

<div class="scored-quiz__actions">
<button type="submit" class="button button-primary">Check answers</button>
<button type="reset" class="button button-secondary">Reset and retry</button>
</div>
